questions.title: Avoiding Reserved SQL Table Names
questions.question: A team is building a backend using SQLAlchemy. They create a model called Order. In many SQL databases, ORDER is a reserved keyword (used in ORDER BY). What is the correct and safe way to handle this?

options.optionText: Leave __tablename__ unset — SQLAlchemy will detect the conflict and automatically choose a safe name
Explicitly set __tablename__ = "orders" — a name that avoids the reserved word
Rename the Python class from Order to OrderModel — this alone fixes the table name conflict
Set __tablename__ = "Order" exactly as the class name — SQLAlchemy automatically escapes reserved words in generated SQL

save_all() automatically detects the conflict and rejects the second thread
Both threads can pass the availability check before either one performs the write, so both may end up marking the same seat as BLOCKED — effectively double-booking
This code is thread-safe, because Python's GIL ensures only one thread runs at a time, so the two threads can never interleave their steps

questions.title: Isolation Level Doesn't Prevent Race
questions.question:
Under an isolation level called REPEATABLE READ (a common default in some relational databases), a transaction is guaranteed not to see changes made by other transactions to rows it has already read, until it re-reads or commits. Consider this timeline between two transactions, T-A and T-B, both updating the same row X:

```
Time 0ms: T-A starts, reads row X: value = AVAILABLE
Time 2ms: T-B starts, reads row X: value = AVAILABLE
Time 4ms: T-A updates row X to BLOCKED, commits successfully
Time 5ms: T-B updates row X to BLOCKED (based on its own earlier read), commits
```
What actually happens at Time 5ms?

options.optionText: T-B's commit also succeeds, because REPEATABLE READ does not stop two separate transactions from each reading the same "before" value and both acting on it
T-B's commit fails automatically, since T-A already changed the row
T-A's commit is retroactively rolled back once T-B commits
Both transactions are blocked from committing until a human manually resolves the conflict

questions.title: Serializable Isolation Definition
questions.question: Which of the following best defines what SERIALIZABLE isolation guarantees in a relational database?

options.optionText: Only one transaction is allowed to be active anywhere in the database at any moment
Transactions are guaranteed to always commit in the exact order they were started
No transaction can ever fail, roll back, or need a retry
The outcome of running transactions concurrently must be equivalent to some valid outcome of running those same transactions one after another, in some order

questions.title: Serializable Allows Unrelated Concurrency
questions.question: Two transactions run under SERIALIZABLE isolation. Transaction 1 updates Row X. Transaction 2, running at the same time, updates a completely different Row Y in the same table — the two rows share no data or relationship. What is the most likely outcome?

options.optionText: Both transactions fail, because SERIALIZABLE permits only one active transaction across the whole database
Both transactions commit successfully and independently, since SERIALIZABLE only prevents conflicts on rows that are actually accessed by both transactions
Only the transaction that started first is allowed to commit
Both commit, but the transaction that commits second silently overwrites data from the first

questions.title: Threading Lock Across Processes
questions.question: A backend application runs as multiple separate server processes (for example, behind a load balancer), all connecting to the same shared database. A developer adds a threading.Lock() inside a booking method, reasoning: "only one thread can hold the lock at a time, so this prevents double-booking." Why does this NOT actually prevent two different server processes from double-booking the same database row?

options.optionText: A threading.Lock() object only coordinates threads within a single process's memory — a lock created in one server process has no effect on threads running in a separate server process
threading.Lock() objects expire automatically after a few milliseconds, so they don't stay held long enough to help
threading.Lock() can only be used with synchronous code, and database calls are always asynchronous
threading.Lock() requires a special database driver to function correctly

questions.title: DTO Boundary Decoupling Benefit
questions.question: A Controller class in a layered backend application accepts a dedicated request object (a DTO — Data Transfer Object) as its parameter, instead of accepting raw domain/model objects directly or a long list of loose primitive parameters. What is the main benefit of this design choice?

options.optionText: DTOs are mandatory for any class that uses an ORM like SQLAlchemy
DTOs make the application run measurably faster, since fewer objects are created in memory
A DTO defines a stable, deliberate contract for exactly what a use case needs — so if the underlying domain models change shape later, callers of the use case aren't automatically broken
DTOs are only useful for return values, not for input parameters

questions.title: SQLAlchemy Automatic Change Tracking
questions.question:
In an application using SQLAlchemy, an object seat was fetched earlier in a session (e.g., session.query(Seat).get(seat_id)). Later in the same function, this code runs:

```python
seat.status = "BLOCKED"
seat.blocked_at = datetime.now()
# ... some other unrelated database operations using the same session ...
session.commit()
```
Notice there is no explicit session.add(seat) or repository.save(seat) call after changing seat.status. What happens when session.commit() runs?

options.optionText: The changes to seat.status and seat.blocked_at are silently lost, since nothing was explicitly re-saved
The commit throws a runtime error, because SQLAlchemy requires every changed object to be explicitly re-added to the session
Only seat.status is saved; seat.blocked_at is ignored because it was set after the first attribute
Both changes are saved automatically — SQLAlchemy tracks changes to objects that were already loaded through the session, and commit() flushes all pending changes together

questions.title: Show-Level Pricing
questions.question: In a booking system, ticket prices are stored in a table keyed on the specific (show, seat_type) pair — meaning every individual show has its own price row per seat type, rather than seat types having one single global price. A theatre now wants weekday GOLD seats priced at ₹250 and weekend GOLD seats priced at ₹400, on the exact same screen. Does this pricing design already support that, with zero code or schema changes?

options.optionText: No — a day_of_week field would need to be added to the seat-type table first
No — the price table is keyed by screen, not by individual show, so all shows on one screen must share the same price
Yes — a weekday show and a weekend show are two different show records, so each one already gets its own (show, seat_type) price row
Only if the pricing function is modified to manually check the day of the week from the show's start time
